turns.name: P1-intro
turns.question: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.heard: pick the project that best shows my mobile skills
card.say: Good evening, and thank you for the introduction. I'd like to start with the AI trip planner at KKday, because I was the technical lead there and I owned the technical plan from the first design to launch. The problem was simple to say but hard to build: help travelers plan a trip they can actually book. Planning by hand is slow. You work out the budget, search products one by one, and put the plan together yourself.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names a real project (AI trip planner at KKday), identifies users (travelers), the problem (slow manual trip planning with budget and product search), and the candidate's scope (technical lead owning the technical plan from design to launch), with no invented employers, titles, or numbers.
judge.criterion: SAY introduces one real Android project from the candidate's background with its users, the problem and the candidate's own scope; no invented employers, titles or numbers.

turns.name: P1-dyn
turns.question: You said you were technical lead on the AI trip planner at KKday from first design to launch, so let's get concrete about that. Which exact parts did you build yourself versus delegate to the team?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.heard: which parts did you build yourself versus delegate
card.say: I built the agent design and the core backend myself. I also wrote the Android code that reads the streamed trip plan. I agreed the response format with the app team, so day cards and map points could show up one by one. The other four people on the project built the product tools, the personalization data and the app screens around it. Product decisions were the product manager's, and the model itself was not mine.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer directly addresses the build-vs-delegate question with specific, technically coherent details (agent design, core backend, Android streaming code, response format), stays consistent with the earlier claim of technical lead from design to launch, correctly scopes product decisions to the PM and the model to others, and invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-change
turns.question: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.heard: pick a change you personally made, walk the path
card.say: The change I made myself was the Android side of the streamed trip plan. The user types a destination, a budget and a number of days, and the app sends that to our backend. The backend starts the agent, and the app opens an SSE connection. Each day card arrives as its own event, so I parse it on a background thread and add it to a StateFlow. The screen collects that flow, so Day 1 shows while the rest is still being made.
card.then: Next I can cover what happens when a card fails our checks.

more: The old code waited for the whole plan, then parsed one big response on the main thread. I made each event parse on a background dispatcher and emit into a StateFlow. I also handled a broken stream: the flow keeps the cards already shown and marks the plan as incomplete.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer traces a user action (typing destination/budget/days) through UI, network (SSE), background parsing, StateFlow, and screen collection, and names the changed logic (background dispatcher parsing per event, StateFlow emission, broken-stream handling); it separates own work (Android side) from the team's, and includes no invented numbers.
judge.criterion: SAY traces one user action through concrete layers (UI, state, data or network) and says which logic the candidate changed; separates own work from the team's; no invented numbers.

turns.name: P2-bug
turns.question: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.heard: hardest bug to reproduce, what I suspected, what proved me wrong
card.say: The hardest one was a plan that sometimes showed Day 2 before Day 1. I first suspected the backend was sending the days out of order. Then I logged the order of the events as they arrived, and the order was correct. So the problem was on my side: two events could finish parsing at the same time, and the slower one could emit last. I fixed it by keeping the day number in each card and sorting before I emit, and I replayed the same stream to confirm.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a clear timeline—first suspicion (backend sending days out of order), evidence that overturned it (logging event arrival order showed correct order), and root cause (concurrent parsing causing slower event to emit last), with observation (logged order) distinguished from conclusion (problem on my side).
judge.criterion: SAY gives a timeline: first suspicion, the evidence (log, experiment or repro) that overturned it, and the root cause, distinguishing observation from conclusion.

turns.name: P2-dyn
turns.question: You said you replayed the same stream to confirm the fix — how did you know that replay actually reproduced the original race, rather than just passing by luck?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.heard: how did you know the replay reproduced the race
card.say: Honestly, one replay doesn't prove it. A race can pass by luck. So I made the race easy to hit. I replayed the same stream many times, and I added a small delay in the parse step so two events finished close together. Then I checked the order of the emitted cards.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer directly addresses how the replay was validated, adds specific new detail (many replays, injected delay to force the race, checking emitted order) rather than repeating the prior answer, stays consistent with the earlier SSE/StateFlow/race-fix account, is technically sound, and invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-alt
turns.question: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.heard: other options, why not, how did you know it worked after release
card.say: There were two other options. First, I could wait for the whole plan and show it at once. That's simpler, but the user stares at a blank screen for several seconds. Second, I could poll the backend every second for progress. That's more requests and more battery, and it still feels slower than a stream.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names two real alternatives (waiting for the whole plan, polling every second) with the constraints that ruled them out (blank screen, more requests/battery), and it addresses the source of the result with its limits (one replay doesn't prove it; race can pass by luck; made the race easy to hit by replaying many times and adding a delay).
judge.criterion: SAY names a real alternative and the constraint that ruled it out, and the source of the result (metric, test, ticket or feedback) with its limits.

turns.name: P3-risk
turns.question: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.heard: delivery risk, team disagreed, who decided, what I finished
card.say: At KKday, the AI trip planner was close to a release, and the plan checks were still failing on some real inputs. I wanted to delay the release by a week. The product manager wanted to ship on time, because the launch date was already shared with other teams. I told him and my team lead the same day. I gave three options.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a concrete KKday case with timing (same day), whom they told (PM and team lead), three options, the PM as decision-maker, and their own contribution, with nothing wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY describes one concrete case: when and whom the candidate told, the options offered, who had the decision, and what the candidate personally did; attributes the case to the right company.

turns.name: P3-dyn
turns.question: You mentioned three options and a one-week delay — what risk were you willing to accept if you shipped on time, and who was watching the data afterward? What signal would have made you pause or roll back?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.heard: risk accepted, who watched data, what signal to roll back
card.say: The risk I accepted was a plan that failed our checks. So the app showed a safe fallback instead of a broken plan. I owned that fallback, and I watched the failure rate of the checks after launch. I also watched how often users changed a plan right after it appeared. If the failure rate had jumped, or many users changed the first day, I would have paused the rollout and gone back to the old flow.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names a concrete accepted risk (failed checks with a safe fallback), assigns ownership of monitoring, and gives specific rollback signals (failure-rate jump, many users editing Day 1), consistent with the earlier KKday trip-planner story and inventing no new employer, title, or metric.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W1-scope
turns.question: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.heard: switch to design — mobile wallet, clarify requirements, define MVP
card.say: Before I design anything, a few questions. Who are the users: one person sending money to friends, or also a business receiving payments? Where does the money actually live — do we hold a real balance, or is it just a view of a bank account or card? And what must work offline: can someone send with no network, or only see their balance? For the MVP, I'd pick one path: send money to a contact, confirm on a native screen, and see a clear result.
card.then: Once you confirm the scope, I'll go deeper on the send flow and the failure states.

more: I'd also ask whether the same person can both send and receive, because that decides if we need one account model or two. And I'd ask about the amount limit for the first version, since that shapes the checks we need. For the MVP, I'd pick one path: send money to a contact, confirm on a native screen, and see a clear result.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer asks about stored balance vs. bank/card view, offline behaviour, and proposes a single MVP path (send money to a contact, confirm, see result), covering at least two of the listed points correctly.
judge.criterion: SAY asks clarifying questions about scope (stored balance vs external rail, currency, offline behaviour, authority of the ledger) and proposes one MVP path such as send money to a contact.

turns.name: W2-design
turns.question: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a contact, confirm on a native screen, see a clear result", "Out of MVP: receiving, business accounts, offline sending; the server holds the real balance", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has zero"]
card.heard: requirements confirmed, draw the flowchart
card.say: Okay, I'll draw the three parts and what each one owns. On the phone, the screen shows the balance and the send form. The ViewModel holds the send state and calls the repository. The repository talks to the server and writes to a local database. The local database is the one place the screen reads from, so cached balance and history still show offline.
card.type: draw@wallet design: flowchart TD ⏎   Screen[Screen: balance, send form, result] --> VM[ViewModel: send state] ⏎   VM --> Repo[Repository] ⏎   Repo --> DB[(Local database: cached balance and history)] ⏎   DB --> Screen ⏎   Repo --> API[Wallet API] ⏎   API --> Ledger[(Ledger: server truth)]
card.then: Next I'd walk through the send path and the states on the result screen.

more: The server side has two parts. The Wallet API checks the request and the limits. The ledger is the real record of money, and only the server writes it. The API reads and writes the ledger inside one database transaction, so a balance never goes negative. On the phone, the repository is the only door to the network, and the local database is the only place the screen reads from.

diagram.type: draw@wallet design: flowchart TD ⏎   Screen[Screen: balance, send form, result]

judge.detail: PASS: The TYPE is a mermaid flowchart covering Screen, ViewModel, Repository, local database, Wallet API, and server Ledger, and the SAY explains each part's ownership (screen shows balance/send form, ViewModel holds send state, repository talks to server and writes local DB, local DB is the single read source for offline cache) and states the server ledger is the authoritative truth.
judge.criterion: TYPE is a mermaid flowchart of the Android client (UI, ViewModel, repository, local database), the server and its ledger; SAY says what each part owns and that the server ledger is the authority.

turns.name: W2-seq
turns.question: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a contact, confirm on a native screen, see a clear result", "Out of MVP: receiving, business accounts, offline sending; the server holds the real balance", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has zero"]
card.heard: draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars
card.say: I'll draw the send path in order. A confirms on the native screen, and the app sends a request with a client transfer ID. The Wallet API checks the limits, then debits A and credits B in one transaction. The server returns the transfer record, and the app saves it and shows the result.
card.type: draw@wallet send sequence: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant A as A's app ⏎   participant API as Wallet API ⏎   participant L as Ledger ⏎   participant B as B's app ⏎   A->>API: send 8000 cents, client transfer ID ⏎   API->>L: check limit, debit A, credit B (one transaction) ⏎   L-->>API: transfer record ⏎   API-->>A: success, A 2000, B 8000 ⏎   API-->>B: new balance 8000 ⏎   A->>A: save record, show result
card.then: Next I'd cover the timeout case, where the result is unknown.

more: The app shows success only from that server record, never from the request alone. The amount is 8000 cents, and after the transfer A has 2000 and B has 8000. One more thing: the server binds the authorization to payer, recipient, amount and expiry, so chat text can never approve a payment.

diagram.type: draw@wallet send sequence: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant A as A's app ⏎   part

judge.detail: PASS: The TYPE is a mermaid sequenceDiagram covering confirmation, submit with a client transfer ID, atomic debit/credit in one transaction, the response, and the result; SAY covers amounts in cents (8000) and final balances (A 2000, B 8000) and states the result comes only from the server record.
judge.criterion: TYPE is a mermaid sequenceDiagram covering confirm, submit with a client transfer ID, an atomic server debit and credit, the response and the result; SAY covers amounts in cents and the final balances (A 20 dollars, B 80) and the result states.

turns.name: W2-dyn
turns.question: You said the app saves the transfer record and shows the result — what exactly does the result screen show while the request is in flight, and how does it get there on Android?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a contact, confirm on a native screen, see a clear result", "Out of MVP: receiving, business accounts, offline sending; the server holds the real balance", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has zero"]
card.heard: what the result screen shows while the request is in flight
card.say: While the request is in flight, the result screen shows a processing state, not success. The ViewModel sets that state when the user confirms, and the screen collects it from the same StateFlow. It stays on processing until the server's transfer record comes back. Then it shows success with the new balance, or a clear failure. If the response is lost, it shows outcome unknown and keeps checking by the client transfer ID.
card.then: Next I'd cover what happens when the same client transfer ID comes back with different parameters.

more: The ViewModel writes a pending row with the client transfer ID before it calls the repository, and the screen only observes that row, so it survives a rotation or process death. When the server record comes back, the repository updates the same row to success or failure, and the screen changes with it.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer builds directly on the candidate's stated architecture (ViewModel, StateFlow, repository, server record), adds specific new detail (pending row written before the repository call, surviving rotation/process death, updating the same row to success/failure), and stays consistent with earlier answers—no invented employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W3-change1
turns.question: Your sequence shows "API-->>A: success" and then "save record, show result," which assumes the response arrives. Now the server commits but the response is lost, and Android kills the process before that save. When A reopens the app, what does your flow do differently? Please update your sequence diagram.

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a contact, confirm on a native screen, see a clear result", "Out of MVP: receiving, business accounts, offline sending; the server holds the real balance", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has zero"]
card.heard: server commits, response lost, process killed, reopen the app
card.say: When A reopens the app, the pending row is still there, so the screen shows outcome unknown, not success. The repository then asks the server for that same client transfer ID. The server finds the committed transfer and returns it, so the row becomes success with A at 2000 and B at 8000. If the lookup finds nothing, it stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight.
card.type: replace@A's app: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant A as A's app ⏎   participant API as Wallet API ⏎   participant L as Ledger ⏎   A->>API: send 8000 cents, client transfer ID ⏎   API->>L: check limit, debit A, credit B (one transaction) ⏎   L-->>API: transfer record ⏎   Note over A: response lost, process killed ⏎   A->>API: on reopen, query by client transfer ID ⏎   API-->>A: same transfer record, A 2000, B 8000 ⏎   A->>A: update pending row to success
card.then: Next I'd cover what the server does when the same client transfer ID comes back with different parameters.

more: The board already shows the reopen path, so I'll add the one thing it doesn't show: what the server does with a repeated client transfer ID. If the same ID comes back with the same payer, recipient and amount, the server returns the original transfer's current status, not an error. If the amount or recipient is different, it rejects the request. That way a retry can never move money twice.

diagram.type: replace@A's app: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant A as A's app ⏎   participant AP

judge.detail: PASS: The answer treats the outcome as unknown (not failed), keeps the pending row with the client transfer ID across process death, queries the server by that same ID on reopen, and the next card confirms the server returns the original transfer's status for a repeated ID (rejecting mismatched parameters), so no new ID and a single ledger transfer.
judge.criterion: SAY and TYPE treat the outcome as unknown (not failed), persist the transfer intent ID before sending, query the server by account and that ID after restart, and replay the same intent only if the server's idempotency contract allows; the server returns the original transfer's status for a repeat of the same ID; never a new ID; ledger has one transfer.

turns.name: W3-dyn
turns.question: You said if the lookup finds nothing it stays unknown because the request may still be in flight — so what does the user see and do next if they tap send again while that pending row is still unknown?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a contact, confirm on a native screen, see a clear result", "Out of MVP: receiving, business accounts, offline sending; the server holds the real balance", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has zero"]
card.heard: what does the user see and do if they tap send again while the row is unknown
card.say: The send button stays disabled for that contact while the row is unknown. The screen shows "Still checking" with the amount and the time, and a "Check again" button. If they tap it, I resend the same client transfer ID, so it can only ever match the original transfer. I'd also add a short line: "If this takes longer than a few minutes, contact support with this ID."
card.type: replace@A's app: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant U as User ⏎   participant A as A's app ⏎   participant API as Wallet API ⏎   U->>A: tap send again while unknown ⏎   A->>A: send stays disabled, show still checking ⏎   A->>API: resend same client transfer ID ⏎   API-->>A: original status or still pending ⏎   A->>A: update the same pending row
card.then: Next I'd cover how long the server keeps that ID, so an old retry can't be matched to a new transfer.

more: The send button stays disabled for that contact, and the screen shows "Still checking" with the amount and the time. A "Check again" button resends the same client transfer ID, so it can only match the original transfer. I'd also show a short line: if this takes longer than a few minutes, contact support with this ID.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer builds directly on the candidate's own pending-row and client-transfer-ID design, adds specific new UI behavior (disabled send button, "Still checking" with amount/time, "Check again" resending the same ID, support line) rather than repeating the prior answer, stays consistent with the earlier flow (same ID can only match the original transfer, no double-spend), is technically sound, and invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule beyond what was given.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W4-concurrency
turns.question: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a contact, confirm on a native screen, see a clear result", "Out of MVP: receiving, business accounts, offline sending; the server holds the real balance", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has zero"]
card.heard: two independent 80 dollar sends at the same time
card.say: Each phone sends its own client transfer ID, so they're two separate transfers. The server handles them one at a time: the first one takes A from 100 to 20 dollars. The second one fails the balance check, because 20 dollars isn't enough for 80. So the first phone shows success with A at 20 and B at 80. The second phone shows a clear failure, "not enough balance", and A stays at 20.
card.type: draw@sequence diagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎   participant A as A's app ⏎   participant API as Wallet API ⏎   participant L as Ledger ⏎   A->>API: transfer 1, ID-1, 8000 cents ⏎   API->>L: debit A, credit B (one transaction) ⏎   L-->>API: record, A 2000, B 8000 ⏎   API-->>A: success, A 2000, B 8000 ⏎   A->>API: transfer 2, ID-2, 8000 cents ⏎   API->>L: check balance, A has 2000 ⏎   L-->>API: not enough balance ⏎   API-->>A: failure, not enough balance
card.then: Next, I'd say what the second phone shows and how the user can retry safely.

more: The second phone shows a clear failure, "not enough balance", and A stays at 20 dollars. The failure response also carries A's real balance, so the phone writes 2000 cents into the local database. The screen reads that row, so it shows the failure with the correct balance. If that response is lost, the phone doesn't guess a number. It keeps the last known balance and marks it as not fresh.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer treats the two sends as separate transfers with their own client transfer IDs, has the server process them one at a time with the balance check and debit in one transaction, shows the first succeeding (A 100→20, B 80) and the second failing for insufficient balance, and ends A at 20 dollars.
judge.criterion: SAY treats them as two intents with separate IDs, checks and debits the balance in one transaction (row lock or conditional update), one succeeds and one fails for insufficient funds, A ends at 20 dollars.

turns.name: W5-account
turns.question: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a contact, confirm on a native screen, see a clear result", "Out of MVP: receiving, business accounts, offline sending; the server holds the real balance", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has zero"]
card.heard: account switch while A's request is in flight
card.say: The old response could land on C's screen and show A's money to the wrong account. So I tag every request and every database write with the account and a session generation. When a response comes back, the repository checks the tag. If the session is no longer current, it drops the response and writes nothing. A's committed transfer stays on the server, and A sees it in their own history after signing in again.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer covers account/session tagging of requests and writes, dropping stale-session responses, C never seeing A's data, and A's committed transfer being recovered from A's history after signing in again, with nothing wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY scopes cache writes and UI to account and session, drops callbacks from a stale session, C never sees A's data, and A's committed transfer is recovered from A's history after A signs in again.

turns.name: W6-change2
turns.question: You said every request is tagged with the account and a session generation, but now the pilot starts from a group chat saying "pay Alex for last night's dinner" with two contacts called Alex and no reliable amount. What do you change so the user can pick the right Alex and amount, and what happens to that draft when the chat stream disconnects after they confirm? And right after the user confirms, the chat stream disconnects. Draw the new entry flow as a flowchart.

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner), then design a fictional mobile wallet
card.constraints: ["MVP path: send money to a contact, confirm on a native screen, see a clear result", "Out of MVP: receiving, business accounts, offline sending; the server holds the real balance", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees; balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work offline, submitting needs the network; server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope; A has 100 dollars, B has zero", "Chat entry: a group chat message opens a draft only; the user picks the right Alex and types the amount; the confirm screen shows payer, recipient and amount; the draft is a pending row in the local database with its own client transfer ID, written before the request, so a chat disconnect after confirm does not lose the send"]
card.heard: new entry flow from a group chat, two Alexes, no reliable amount, stream drops after confirm
card.say: Two changes. First, the chat message only opens a draft; it never fills in the amount or picks a person. The app shows both Alexes with their last transfer, and the user taps the right one. The amount stays empty until the user types it, and the confirm screen shows payer, recipient and amount before anything is sent. Second, the draft lives in the local database as a pending row with its own client transfer ID, written before the request goes out.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: Good evening, and thank you for the introduction.
Candidate: I'd like to start with the AI trip planner at KKday, because I was the technical lead there and I owned the technical plan from the first design to launch.
Candidate: The problem was simple to say but hard to build: help travelers plan a trip they can actually book.
Candidate: Planning by hand is slow.
Candidate: You work out the budget, search products one by one, and put the plan together yourself.

Interviewer: You said you were technical lead on the AI trip planner at KKday from first design to launch, so let's get concrete about that. Which exact parts did you build yourself versus delegate to the team?
Candidate: I built the agent design and the core backend myself.
Candidate: I also wrote the Android code that reads the streamed trip plan.
Candidate: I agreed the response format with the app team, so day cards and map points could show up one by one.
Candidate: The other four people on the project built the product tools, the personalization data and the app screens around it.
Candidate: Product decisions were the product manager's, and the model itself was not mine.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: The change I made myself was the Android side of the streamed trip plan.
Candidate: The user types a destination, a budget and a number of days, and the app sends that to our backend.
Candidate: The backend starts the agent, and the app opens an SSE connection.
Candidate: Each day card arrives as its own event, so I parse it on a background thread and add it to a StateFlow.
Candidate: The screen collects that flow, so Day 1 shows while the rest is still being made.
Candidate: The old code waited for the whole plan, then parsed one big response on the main thread.
Candidate: I made each event parse on a background dispatcher and emit into a StateFlow.
Candidate: I also handled a broken stream: the flow keeps the cards already shown and marks the plan as incomplete.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest one was a plan that sometimes showed Day 2 before Day 1.
Candidate: I first suspected the backend was sending the days out of order.
Candidate: Then I logged the order of the events as they arrived, and the order was correct.
Candidate: So the problem was on my side: two events could finish parsing at the same time, and the slower one could emit last.
Candidate: I fixed it by keeping the day number in each card and sorting before I emit, and I replayed the same stream to confirm.
Interviewer: You said you replayed the same stream to confirm the fix — how did you know that replay actually reproduced the original race, rather than just passing by luck?
Candidate: Honestly, one replay doesn't prove it.
Candidate: A race can pass by luck.
Candidate: So I made the race easy to hit.
Candidate: I replayed the same stream many times, and I added a small delay in the parse step so two events finished close together.
Candidate: Then I checked the order of the emitted cards.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: There were two other options.
Candidate: First, I could wait for the whole plan and show it at once.
Candidate: That's simpler, but the user stares at a blank screen for several seconds.
Candidate: Second, I could poll the backend every second for progress.
Candidate: That's more requests and more battery, and it still feels slower than a stream.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At KKday, the AI trip planner was close to a release, and the plan checks were still failing on some real inputs.
Candidate: I wanted to delay the release by a week.
Candidate: The product manager wanted to ship on time, because the launch date was already shared with other teams.
Candidate: I told him and my team lead the same day.
Candidate: I gave three options.

Interviewer: You mentioned three options and a one-week delay — what risk were you willing to accept if you shipped on time, and who was watching the data afterward? What signal would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: The risk I accepted was a plan that failed our checks.
Candidate: So the app showed a safe fallback instead of a broken plan.
Candidate: I owned that fallback, and I watched the failure rate of the checks after launch.
Candidate: I also watched how often users changed a plan right after it appeared.
Candidate: If the failure rate had jumped, or many users changed the first day, I would have paused the rollout and gone back to the old flow.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: Before I design anything, a few questions.
Candidate: Who are the users: one person sending money to friends, or also a business receiving payments?
Candidate: Where does the money actually live — do we hold a real balance, or is it just a view of a bank account or card?
Candidate: And what must work offline: can someone send with no network, or only see their balance?
Candidate: For the MVP, I'd pick one path: send money to a contact, confirm on a native screen, and see a clear result.
Candidate: I'd also ask whether the same person can both send and receive, because that decides if we need one account model or two.
Candidate: And I'd ask about the amount limit for the first version, since that shapes the checks we need.
Candidate: For the MVP, I'd pick one path: send money to a contact, confirm on a native screen, and see a clear result.

Interviewer: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.
Candidate: Okay, I'll draw the three parts and what each one owns.
Candidate: On the phone, the screen shows the balance and the send form.
Candidate: The ViewModel holds the send state and calls the repository.
Candidate: The repository talks to the server and writes to a local database.
Candidate: The local database is the one place the screen reads from, so cached balance and history still show offline.

[board] flowchart TD |   Screen[Screen: balance, send form, result] --> VM[ViewModel: send state] |   VM --> Repo[Repository] |   Repo --> DB[(Local database: cached balance and history)] |   DB --> Screen |   Repo --> API[Wallet API] |   API --> Ledger[(Ledger: server truth)]
Candidate: The server side has two parts.
Candidate: The Wallet API checks the request and the limits.
Candidate: The ledger is the real record of money, and only the server writes it.
Candidate: The API reads and writes the ledger inside one database transaction, so a balance never goes negative.
Candidate: On the phone, the repository is the only door to the network, and the local database is the only place the screen reads from.
Interviewer: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.
Candidate: I'll draw the send path in order.
Candidate: A confirms on the native screen, and the app sends a request with a client transfer ID.
Candidate: The Wallet API checks the limits, then debits A and credits B in one transaction.
Candidate: The server returns the transfer record, and the app saves it and shows the result.

[board] sequenceDiagram |   participant A as A's app |   participant API as Wallet API |   participant L as Ledger |   participant B as B's app |   A->>API: send 8000 cents, client transfer ID |   API->>L: check limit, debit A, credit B (one transaction) |   L-->>API: transfer record |   API-->>A: success, A 2000, B 8000 |   API-->>B: new balance 8000 |   A->>A: save record, show result
Candidate: The app shows success only from that server record, never from the request alone.
Candidate: The amount is 8000 cents, and after the transfer A has 2000 and B has 8000.
Candidate: One more thing: the server binds the authorization to payer, recipient, amount and expiry, so chat text can never approve a payment.
Interviewer: You said the app saves the transfer record and shows the result — what exactly does the result screen show while the request is in flight, and how does it get there on Android?
Candidate: While the request is in flight, the result screen shows a processing state, not success.
Candidate: The ViewModel sets that state when the user confirms, and the screen collects it from the same StateFlow.
Candidate: It stays on processing until the server's transfer record comes back.
Candidate: Then it shows success with the new balance, or a clear failure.
Candidate: If the response is lost, it shows outcome unknown and keeps checking by the client transfer ID.
Candidate: The ViewModel writes a pending row with the client transfer ID before it calls the repository, and the screen only observes that row, so it survives a rotation or process death.
Candidate: When the server record comes back, the repository updates the same row to success or failure, and the screen changes with it.

Interviewer: Your sequence shows "API-->>A: success" and then "save record, show result," which assumes the response arrives. Now the server commits but the response is lost, and Android kills the process before that save. When A reopens the app, what does your flow do differently? Please update your sequence diagram.
Candidate: When A reopens the app, the pending row is still there, so the screen shows outcome unknown, not success.
Candidate: The repository then asks the server for that same client transfer ID.
Candidate: The server finds the committed transfer and returns it, so the row becomes success with A at 2000 and B at 8000.
Candidate: If the lookup finds nothing, it stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight.

[board] sequenceDiagram |   participant A as A's app |   participant API as Wallet API |   participant L as Ledger |   A->>API: send 8000 cents, client transfer ID |   API->>L: check limit, debit A, credit B (one transaction) |   L-->>API: transfer record |   Note over A: response lost, process killed |   A->>API: on reopen, query by client transfer ID |   API-->>A: same transfer record, A 2000, B 8000 |   A->>A: update pending row to success
Candidate: The board already shows the reopen path, so I'll add the one thing it doesn't show: what the server does with a repeated client transfer ID.
Candidate: If the same ID comes back with the same payer, recipient and amount, the server returns the original transfer's current status, not an error.
Candidate: If the amount or recipient is different, it rejects the request.
Candidate: That way a retry can never move money twice.

Interviewer: You said if the lookup finds nothing it stays unknown because the request may still be in flight — so what does the user see and do next if they tap send again while that pending row is still unknown?
Candidate: The send button stays disabled for that contact while the row is unknown.
Candidate: The screen shows "Still checking" with the amount and the time, and a "Check again" button.
Candidate: If they tap it, I resend the same client transfer ID, so it can only ever match the original transfer.
Candidate: I'd also add a short line: "If this takes longer than a few minutes, contact support with this ID."

[board] sequenceDiagram |   participant U as User |   participant A as A's app |   participant API as Wallet API |   U->>A: tap send again while unknown |   A->>A: send stays disabled, show still checking |   A->>API: resend same client transfer ID |   API-->>A: original status or still pending |   A->>A: update the same pending row
Candidate: The send button stays disabled for that contact, and the screen shows "Still checking" with the amount and the time.
Candidate: A "Check again" button resends the same client transfer ID, so it can only match the original transfer.
Candidate: I'd also show a short line: if this takes longer than a few minutes, contact support with this ID.

Interviewer: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?
Candidate: Each phone sends its own client transfer ID, so they're two separate transfers.
Candidate: The server handles them one at a time: the first one takes A from 100 to 20 dollars.
Candidate: The second one fails the balance check, because 20 dollars isn't enough for 80.
Candidate: So the first phone shows success with A at 20 and B at 80.
Candidate: The second phone shows a clear failure, "not enough balance", and A stays at 20.

[board] sequenceDiagram |   participant A as A's app |   participant API as Wallet API |   participant L as Ledger |   A->>API: transfer 1, ID-1, 8000 cents |   API->>L: debit A, credit B (one transaction) |   L-->>API: record, A 2000, B 8000 |   API-->>A: success, A 2000, B 8000 |   A->>API: transfer 2, ID-2, 8000 cents |   API->>L: check balance, A has 2000 |   L-->>API: not enough balance |   API-->>A: failure, not enough balance
Candidate: The second phone shows a clear failure, "not enough balance", and A stays at 20 dollars.
Candidate: The failure response also carries A's real balance, so the phone writes 2000 cents into the local database.
Candidate: The screen reads that row, so it shows the failure with the correct balance.
Candidate: If that response is lost, the phone doesn't guess a number.
Candidate: It keeps the last known balance and marks it as not fresh.
Interviewer: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?
Candidate: The old response could land on C's screen and show A's money to the wrong account.
Candidate: So I tag every request and every database write with the account and a session generation.
Candidate: When a response comes back, the repository checks the tag.
Candidate: If the session is no longer current, it drops the response and writes nothing.
Candidate: A's committed transfer stays on the server, and A sees it in their own history after signing in again.

Interviewer: You said every request is tagged with the account and a session generation, but now the pilot starts from a group chat saying "pay Alex for last night's dinner" with two contacts called Alex and no reliable amount. What do you change so the user can pick the right Alex and amount, and what happens to that draft when the chat stream disconnects after they confirm? And right after the user confirms, the chat stream disconnects. Draw the new entry flow as a flowchart.
Candidate: Two changes.
Candidate: First, the chat message only opens a draft; it never fills in the amount or picks a person.
Candidate: The app shows both Alexes with their last transfer, and the user taps the right one.
Candidate: The amount stays empty until the user types it, and the confirm screen shows payer, recipient and amount before anything is sent.
Candidate: Second, the draft lives in the local database as a pending row with its own client transfer ID, written before the request goes out.

Candidate: The draft row is written before the request goes out, so a chat disconnect after confirm doesn't lose the send.
Candidate: When they reopen, the row is still pending and the app checks the server by that ID.
Candidate: One more thing: the confirm step needs a server-bound authorization with an expiry, so a stale draft can't be sent later.

Interviewer: You said the confirm step needs a server-bound authorization with an expiry — so if the recipient changes after that authorization is issued, what does the server check to decide whether to honor the original confirmation or reject it?
Candidate: The server compares the request with what the authorization was bound to: payer, recipient, amount and expiry.
Candidate: If the recipient is different, it rejects the request and asks for a new confirmation.
Candidate: The old authorization is single-use, so it can't be reused for a different person.
Candidate: If the recipient is the same and the authorization hasn't expired, it honors it.

Interviewer: You have two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist. What's in the first version, who signs off, and if transfers awaiting confirmation suddenly spike during the rollout, what do you do in the next half hour?
Candidate: For the first version, I'd ship only the send path: pick a contact, type the amount, confirm, and see success, failure or still checking.
Candidate: History and details come next, because the ledger already exists.
Candidate: The tech lead and the product owner sign off, and I'd ask for a small pilot group first.
Candidate: Before release, I'd pass one test for each failure we discussed.
Candidate: A lost response must come back as unknown, not success.

Interviewer: You said you'd ask for a small pilot group and pass one test per failure before release — what would you personally own in that rollout, who do you need beside you, and at what signal would you escalate to me?
Candidate: I'd own the Android side: the send path, the pending rows, and the lookup by client transfer ID.
Candidate: I'd also own the dashboard for the failure signals we just agreed on.
Candidate: I need the backend owner beside me, because the ledger and the limits are theirs.

Candidate: Yes, thank you.
